name: Hassan Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to employers, AI firms or political parties. This is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Hassan, 43, and I lead an excavator crew at a large limestone mine. My two-year technical diploma helps when I'm explaining the machine drawings, but most of my shift is still digging and watching the working face for loose rock. We're at a low-paying mine, and with a mortgage, two school-age children and less than a month saved, I can't ignore a short pay packet. My partner works mornings in a bakery; similar mining jobs nearby are scarce. I use AI every day to turn my own rough study notes into questions, but never as permission to operate a machine; teaching an apprentice properly is the bit I like most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew to take whatever small saving helps and stop expecting a miracle. If AI can tidy a handover note, fine, but it hasn't filled a bucket. I'd rather share a useful trick than sit through another big presentation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The AI part of that picture doesn't frighten me much, but the household budget does. We paid for a leaking hot-water tank last month and I can still see the dent in our savings. If one of us loses a few shifts, the mortgage will feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll carry on leading the excavator shifts and checking the working face myself. Starting this week I'll cancel two unused subscriptions and put the 18 a month into our emergency account. Through the first year I'll keep using AI for study questions at home, checking the answers against my actual course notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the money, not dazzled or terrified by the software. I like finding something I can improve today. A cancelled subscription won't replace a wage, but seeing the balance rise would stop me feeling stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use AI without relying on it for mine safety?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I put a paragraph from my own notes in and ask for three questions, then answer without looking. If the answer looks wrong, I check the notes rather than trust the machine. I don't put mine records or safety instructions into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say about the savings plan at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would keep a small repair account rather than spend the saving on another treat. The children don't need to hear every worry, but I'd explain why we're using the library more. My excavator shift pays the mortgage, and a broken water tank can still empty our cushion.

say: I welcome **small savings** from AI but would rather share a useful trick than hear another presentation.
I still see **digging and checking** as hands-on work that a tidy handover note cannot replace.
think: I worry that **lost shifts** would reach the mortgage before we rebuilt the repair money.
I know **AI study tools** do not change the thin savings left after replacing our water tank.
do: Keep leading **excavator shifts** and personally check the working face before digging starts.
Cancel two **unused subscriptions** and transfer 18 monthly to the emergency account through the first year.
feel: I feel **anxious** about household money, but making one small improvement keeps me from feeling stuck.
S0.quote: My excavator shift pays the mortgage, and a broken water tank can still empty our cushion.
fieldNote: His daily **AI use** is confined to study support, with explicit checking; it does not imply careless use around heavy equipment.
His anxiety precedes major **automation**, arising from repair costs, scarce alternative employers and two earners whose shifts both matter.

steps.text: Keep leading excavator shifts and checking the working face personally
Cancel two unused subscriptions and transfer 18 monthly into emergency savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should learn how the new planning works before somebody uses it to blame the crew. A loading order can look clever and still ignore wet ground. I'd ask to help test it, with operators able to reject an unsafe instruction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning and ordering will change before a robot can do all my excavator work in this picture. I'm interested, but fewer planning staff could mean the crew carries more checking without more pay. Our household can't absorb a quiet reduction in shifts just because I'm keen on new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for two paid sessions on the new planning system and compare its suggestions with what happens on our actual shifts. I'll also ask our union representative to collect operators' concerns about hours before the trial expands. In the first year I'd keep the subscription saving and show the representative any shift losses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious and curious at once. I can see a chance to make myself useful, but curiosity isn't a guarantee of hours. I don't want the younger drivers thinking they have to agree with every screen to look willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring to a trial meeting as evidence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd record a route suggestion that would put the excavator on ground we'd closed off after rain. Then I'd take it to the trial meeting and ask how the system should have caught it. I would want a correction, not a contest about who sounds cleverer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you stop your enthusiasm hiding the household risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner what the next rota actually says before changing our spending again. We've already cut the unused subscriptions in the first picture. I can learn a planning screen, but I can't learn my way out of an unpaid shift.

say: I want **operators testing** the planning system and retaining the right to reject unsafe instructions.
I would challenge **bad suggestions** with evidence from shifts, rather than treat the trial as a competition.
think: I expect **planning changes** sooner than robot digging, with extra checking potentially added to our crew.
I know **learning quickly** cannot guarantee paid hours or protect the mortgage from a smaller rota.
do: Request two **paid sessions** to compare planning suggestions with actual excavator shifts and ground conditions.
Ask the **union representative** to collect concerns about hours before the trial expands across the mine.
feel: I feel **anxious and curious**, interested in useful tools but alert to what enthusiasm cannot protect.
S1.quote: I can learn a planning screen, but I can't learn my way out of an unpaid shift.
fieldNote: His interest in **testing software** is paired with a specific safety example and does not remove concern about his own earnings.
He involves the **union** before the trial expands, connecting individual learning with collective scrutiny of the resulting hours and workload.

steps.text: Request two paid sessions testing planning suggestions against actual excavator shifts
Ask the union representative to collect crew concerns about paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the warning has two dates: thinking work in 2028 and robot digging around 2031. We should use the first to learn while bargaining over the second. I'd ask the company to offer operators paid places with the people testing the equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose my excavator seat once the robots match us, and there aren't spare mines down the road. I think I have a chance of moving into equipment testing because I already teach operators and study willingly. That's a chance I need to test, not a job I've secretly already got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask to spend one paid shift alongside the mine's equipment testing crew and find out their entry requirements. I'll ask the union to bargain for operators to get first access to paid training. In the first year after AGI arrives I'd apply for a testing placement, keeping my current shifts unless an actual offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, especially when I picture the mortgage after 2031. I haven't reached the point of thinking the wage is certain to vanish, because I can see a possible move within the mine. I do know that being quick with a tool won't make a vacancy appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test whether the proposed move is real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the testing crew what the work really involves, how many places exist and whether operator experience counts. I'd want to hear something less flattering than 'people like you will be fine'. My children eat actual dinners, not compliments about my adaptability.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you promise your partner tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner that I'm applying for something, not promise I've saved the household already. We'd keep the emergency saving and avoid borrowing for a private course. If no paid place appeared, I'd go back to the union and ask for a transition payment rather than hide the problem.

say: I want **paid testing places** offered to operators while the company prepares for robot equipment.
I would distinguish **2028 planning** from robot digging around 2031 when discussing the warning with the crew.
think: I could lose the **excavator seat**, but teaching experience may help me compete for equipment testing work.
I know a **possible transfer** is neither a vacancy nor a guarantee that our mortgage remains affordable.
do: Request one **paid shadow shift** with equipment testers and ask about their actual entry requirements.
Seek **union-backed training access** and apply for a testing placement after AGI arrives, keeping current shifts meanwhile.
feel: I feel **anxious** about 2031, while seeing a possible move that I still need to prove exists.
S2.quote: My children eat actual dinners, not compliments about my adaptability.
fieldNote: His mood reflects **credible risk**, with agency grounded in relevant teaching experience rather than certainty of a future testing job.
He separates **applications from promises** at home and refuses debt-funded training, recognising how little reserve his household can risk.

steps.text: Request a paid shadow shift with the equipment testing crew
Ask the union to bargain for operators first access to paid training
Apply for a testing placement without leaving paid excavator shifts prematurely

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew five years is enough to demand training before the last-minute panic. Thinking AI in 2031 changes planning, then robots around 2034 reach the digging itself. I'd still ask for operators to help decide how those stages are handled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra three years before AGI compared with the fast picture let me build a record of doing more than operating. I could test whether equipment trials suit me while the mine still needs my normal work. I'd be about 51 at the robot stage, so I still need a wage rather than a retirement slogan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for one paid equipment trial shift each month and keep a record of what I learn, without using AI to invent the results. We'll add 30 a month to the emergency account after the subscription saving. In the first year after AGI arrives I'd apply for an internal testing role if the supervised trial work has gone well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, but the risk feels like something I can work on over years. The wider warning matters more than another clever study app. I can try a route, find out it isn't for me, and still have time to look again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an internal offer worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the pay and hours as well as the job title. A testing role with fewer paid shifts might leave us worse off despite sounding like progress. I'd ask my partner to work through the household budget with the actual offer in front of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the first role you try does not suit you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the trial role didn't fit, I'd stop calling it the answer and ask about another paid route. I wouldn't spend five years defending my first idea just because I'd said it in front of the crew. Five years gives me room to be wrong before the mortgage has to pay for my mistake.

say: I would demand **early training** rather than wait until robot equipment is nearly ready for the mine.
I want **operators involved** in planning both the thinking-AI stage and the later replacement of digging work.
think: I can build **trial experience** before robots arrive, but at about 51 I will still need earnings.
I judge **internal offers** by actual pay and hours, not whether a new title sounds like progress.
do: Request a **monthly paid trial shift** and keep an honest record of the practical work learned.
Add **30 monthly** to emergency savings and apply for a testing role after successful supervised trials.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with room to test a route and change course before our mortgage depends on it.
S3.quote: Five years gives me room to be wrong before the mortgage has to pay for my mistake.
fieldNote: He uses the additional **warning time** to test a career route while paid work continues, rather than assuming general adaptability is enough.
His focus on **pay and hours** guards against treating a better-sounding job as an improvement for a household with thin savings.

steps.text: Request one paid equipment trial shift each month
Add 30 monthly to emergency savings beyond the subscription saving
Apply for a testing role after successful supervised trial work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a chance to change who gets the new jobs, not just how fast we buy machines. AGI in 2036 and robots around 2039 give time for a proper operator training route. I'd keep asking the union to get that route written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about 56 when robots reach the digging, with the children grown. I could spend years getting good at testing equipment before then instead of chasing one vacancy at the last minute. I still can't assume testing is untouched by thinking AI or that the mine employs me forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll start with the monthly paid trial shifts rather than wait for the decade to pass. As experience builds I'd apply for suitable internal posts and keep adding the extra 30 a month to our reserve. In the first year after thinking AI arrives I'd review which parts of testing still need people and ask for paid practice in those tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about earning in my fifties, but I can imagine an ordinary day on the other side of a job change. That's different from staring at a deadline. I'd still want to check the budget instead of spending as though a decade were a savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about their own work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children to get broad skills and try real work before choosing a path. I wouldn't push them into mining just because I know the gate supervisor. They'll have their own lives, and I don't want my fear to choose their subjects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the training route fair for the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want any training agreement to include the next group of operators, not just the loud ones who volunteer first. I'm quick to put my hand up, and that could leave a quieter colleague behind. A mine should not call a lucky transfer a plan for the whole crew.

say: I want a **written operator route** into new work while there is time to prepare it properly.
I would argue that **quieter colleagues** need training access too, rather than rewarding only the first volunteers.
think: I could build **testing experience** over years, but neither the role nor the employer is guaranteed forever.
I expect **grown children** to change household demands while I still need to earn when robots arrive.
do: Begin **monthly paid trials** now and apply for suitable internal posts as experience builds.
Keep saving **30 extra monthly** and review which testing tasks need people after thinking AI arrives.
feel: I feel **anxious** about later earnings, with a clearer picture of life after a possible job change.
S4.quote: A mine should not call a lucky transfer a plan for the whole crew.
fieldNote: His progressive outlook appears through **fair access**, including colleagues less willing to volunteer, rather than through a generic political statement.
He treats the decade as **time for practice**, while acknowledging that testing work itself could change once thinking AI arrives.

steps.text: Begin monthly paid equipment trials and review changing testing tasks after AGI
Continue adding 30 extra monthly to the household emergency reserve
Ask the union to secure written training access for all operators

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I might have to prove myself for another role before we've rebuilt the savings. Paid time with the testing crew and fair access to actual vacancies would help. I'd also want the union to negotiate money for people who do lose their jobs, because not everyone can transfer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether liking technology makes somebody feel safe. It doesn't, at least for me. I can be keen to learn and still need someone to explain how next month's mortgage gets paid.

headlineQuote: I can be keen to learn and still need someone to explain how next month's mortgage gets paid.
portrait: Hassan is a **43-year-old excavator crew leader** with a technical diploma, a mortgage and two school-age children.
He uses **AI daily** for checked study questions while keeping mine records and safety decisions out of the tool.
His **thin reserve** and low mine wage create anxiety even when AI brings little change to the digging itself.
He pursues **paid testing experience** and union-backed access to new roles, using longer warnings for trials rather than claiming certain protection.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could force a rapid job change before the household has rebuilt its emergency savings.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid testing experience**, fair access to actual vacancies and negotiated support for operators who cannot transfer.
